title: Manifesto of the Communist Party
author: Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels
intro: A pamphlet written for a small league of German workers that became one of the most read political texts in history. Start with section one, a portrait of capitalism as a revolutionary force.

title: Wage Labour and Capital
author: Karl Marx
intro: Lectures Marx gave to German workers in Brussels explaining in plain language what wages are and where profit comes from. The best first step toward Capital.

title: Value, Price and Profit
author: Karl Marx
intro: A talk to the First International arguing that unions can and should fight for higher wages, and explaining the theory of surplus value along the way.

title: Theses on Feuerbach
author: Karl Marx
intro: Eleven short notes, ending with the famous line that philosophers have only interpreted the world, while the point is to change it.

title: The Eighteenth Brumaire of Louis Bonaparte
author: Karl Marx
wiki: The Eighteenth Brumaire of Louis Bonaparte
intro: How a failed revolution ended in a nephew of Napoleon seizing power. Marx’s sharpest piece of political history, and the source of “first as tragedy, then as farce.”

title: The Civil War in France
author: Karl Marx
intro: Marx’s account of the Paris Commune, written for the International while the bodies were still being counted. It shaped every later debate about what a workers’ state would look like.

title: Critique of the Gotha Programme
author: Karl Marx
intro: Marx’s notes on a German socialist party program, including his clearest sketch of a communist society: from each according to ability, to each according to needs.

title: Capital, Volume One, Chapter 10: The Working Day
author: Karl Marx
intro: The chapter where Capital comes alive: factory inspectors’ reports on child labor and the long fight to limit the working day. Readable on its own.

title: The Condition of the Working Class in England
author: Friedrich Engels
wiki: The Condition of the Working Class in England
intro: Engels, at 24, walked the slums of Manchester and wrote what he saw. Read the chapter on the great towns.

title: Socialism: Utopian and Scientific
author: Friedrich Engels
intro: The short introduction to Marxism that most socialists of the 1880s and 1890s actually read.

title: The Right to Be Lazy
author: Paul Lafargue
intro: Marx’s son-in-law argues, with jokes, that the labor movement should fight for less work rather than the right to more of it.

title: Useful Work versus Useless Toil
author: William Morris
intro: Morris asks what work would be like if it were done for use and pleasure rather than profit.

title: Reform or Revolution
author: Rosa Luxemburg
intro: Luxemburg’s answer to the argument that socialism could arrive through gradual reforms alone.

title: The Mass Strike
author: Rosa Luxemburg
wiki: The Mass Strike, the Political Party and the Trade Unions
intro: Written after the 1905 revolution in Russia, it argues that mass strikes grow out of struggle rather than being called on command.

title: The Junius Pamphlet
author: Rosa Luxemburg
intro: Written in prison against the First World War, with its famous choice between socialism and barbarism.

title: The Social Basis of the Woman Question
author: Alexandra Kollontai
intro: Kollontai argues that women’s liberation depends on the liberation of labor, and takes on the middle-class feminism of her time.

title: Imperialism, the Highest Stage of Capitalism
author: Vladimir Lenin
wiki: Imperialism, the Highest Stage of Capitalism
intro: Lenin’s account of how monopoly and finance capital drove the great powers to carve up the world.

title: The State and Revolution
author: Vladimir Lenin
intro: Written between the February and October revolutions, it asks what workers should do with the state once they take power.

title: Statement to the Court
author: Eugene V. Debs
intro: Debs’s speech on being sentenced to ten years for opposing the First World War: while there is a lower class, I am in it.

title: Fascism
author: Clara Zetkin
intro: An early Marxist analysis of fascism, delivered months after Mussolini took power, warning that it drew its strength from a desperate middle class.

title: Labour in Irish History
author: James Connolly
intro: Connolly retells Irish history from the side of the poor, arguing that the national and the social question are one.

title: The Transitional Program
author: Leon Trotsky
intro: Trotsky’s program for linking everyday demands to the struggle for power, written on the eve of the Second World War.

title: The Weapon of Theory
author: Amílcar Cabral
intro: Cabral’s speech at the Tricontinental Conference in Havana on why national liberation movements need their own theory, rooted in their own history.

title: The Souls of Black Folk
author: W. E. B. Du Bois
intro: Essays on Black life after Reconstruction that introduced the idea of double consciousness.

title: A Vindication of the Rights of Woman
author: Mary Wollstonecraft
wiki: A Vindication of the Rights of Woman
intro: The founding argument that women are not naturally inferior but deprived of education.

title: Common Sense
author: Thomas Paine
intro: The pamphlet that persuaded ordinary colonists to break with the king, written for readers in plain language.

title: The Soul of Man under Socialism
author: Oscar Wilde
wiki: The Soul of Man Under Socialism
intro: Wilde argues that socialism would free people to become fully themselves, and that charity only prolongs the disease it treats.

title: Civil Disobedience
author: Henry David Thoreau
intro: Written after a night in jail for refusing to pay taxes that supported slavery and the war on Mexico.

title: The Iron Heel
author: Jack London
intro: A novel imagining an American oligarchy crushing the labor movement, written decades before the word totalitarian existed.

title: The Jungle
author: Upton Sinclair
intro: Sinclair aimed at readers’ hearts with the lives of Chicago meatpacking workers and, as he said, hit them in the stomach instead.
